tier_reason: The mechanics meet A: the harness is public (kernels/reference/cublas_hgemm/bench.cu runs cublasGemmEx, FP16 in, FP32 out, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F_FAST_16F; kernels/gemm/hgemm/bench for the project kernel). Makefile flags are -arch=sm_86 -O2, the toolchain is CUDA 13.2 and the GPU is named. But the only winning rows pair stale native-boost project readings (31,875 / 31,765 GFLOPS) with a cuBLAS reading taken on another date. The repo's own docs/inventory.md footnote and issue #167 say that HGEMM figure is disputed and not reproducible, and the current data/baselines.json puts the kernel at about 1.02x cuBLAS under a 1605 MHz clock lock and below cuBLAS at native boost. So the faster-than-cuBLAS claim is first-party and unsettled: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: docs/comparison_to_sota.md: HGEMM 16-warp 2048^3 31,875 GFLOPS vs cuBLAS 28,631 GFLOPS (111.3%); 4096^3 31,765 vs 29,708 GFLOPS (106.9%). Losing rows on the same page: IGEMM pipelined cp.async 4096^3 20.23 vs 29.44 TOPS cuBLAS (68.7%); sparse IGEMM tiled 31.59 vs 124.28 TOPS (25.4%) at 2048^3 and 30.89 vs 170.11 TOPS (18.2%) at 4096^3 vs cuSPARSELt; conv2d implicit GEMM 7,150 vs 16,910 GFLOPS cuDNN (42.3%). The project's current data/baselines.json replaces the HGEMM 'Ours' readings with clock-locked (1605 MHz) medians of 29,174 GFLOPS at 2048^3 and 30,401 at 4096^3, about 1.02x the cuBLAS reference (derived from page data). Its notes record native-boost re-measurements of 28,090 and 27,307 GFLOPS, about 0.98x and 0.92x of cuBLAS (derived from page data).
corrections.hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 Ti Laptop GPU (GA104, sm_86, 46 SMs) under a 150 W VBIOS cap, WSL2 on a Windows host; current project HGEMM baselines were measured under a host-side 1605 MHz SM clock lock (nvidia-smi -lgc), while the cuBLAS reference (recorded 2026-05-18) carries no clock-lock note; host CPU not stated
corrections.caveats: The win over cuBLAS is not settled. The two HGEMM rows that beat cuBLAS use native-boost readings that the repo itself disputes: the docs/inventory.md footnote says 'Do not quote it as a settled result', and issue #167 is titled 'hgemm_16warp has two canonical numbers'. Issue #158 records the kernel running slower at native boost than under a clock lock, and #159 records a 4.9% swing between two locked sessions. With the current locked baselines the margin is about 2%, inside that spread. At native boost the kernel measures below the cuBLAS reference. Project and cuBLAS numbers were taken on different dates and under different clock regimes. Every other row on the page loses: dense INT8 68.7% of cuBLAS, sparse INT8 25.4% and 18.2% of cuSPARSELt, conv2d 42.3% of cuDNN. This is a single laptop GPU with a power cap, the README says several results are n=1, and host CPU is not stated. Flash Attention and GroupNorm have no local reference ('not measured locally'). The like-for-like part holds: both sides take FP16 inputs and accumulate and write FP32.

notes: Numbers in claimed_speedup match comparison_to_sota.md exactly, but the repo's own data/baselines.json, the docs/inventory.md footnote and issue #167 (closed by PR #206, opened on github.com) contradict the headline. Recordable shortcoming: claim not reproducible per the project's own tracker; margin at most about 2% under a clock lock and negative at native boost. tier_reason: method_and_result.md gives per-size kernel times for the project and PyTorch fp16 matmul on P100 and RTX 3090. Both sides are public: baseline.py (torch a.matmul(b), 10,000 iterations under nsys) and test_gemv.cu/fast_gemv.cu with a correctness check. The Makefile states the nvcc flags (-O3 -m64 -std=c++17, sm_60/70/75/86), the README pins CUDA 11.7 and Nsight Systems 2023.1.2, and both GPUs and their launch configurations are named. That meets A under the wave's GPU-kernel precedent; the PyTorch version and host CPU are missing.

corrections.caveats: Benchmarks date from May-June 2023 against the PyTorch (and the cuBLAS it dispatches to) of that time; the PyTorch version is not stated and newer releases may have closed the gap. The 2.7x peak is a single size (n=8192 on a P100), where the PyTorch baseline dips to 202 GB/s against 333 GB/s at n=4096. On the 3090 the fp16 gain is 1.02x at n=8192 (156448.3 vs 159163.1 ns) and 1.13x at n=2048 (12395.4 vs 13971.8 ns), both derived from page data, peaking at 1.40x at n=1024. Launch configurations are hand-tuned per size and per GPU. The int8/int4 columns move far fewer bytes than the fp16 PyTorch baseline, so they are not like-for-like. The README names a 3090 Ti while the results document says 3090. Timings are Nsight Systems kernel averages, not end-to-end wall clock. Host CPU not stated.
